case_name: CASE OF ARVANITIS AND PHILELEFTHEROS PUBLIC COMPANY LIMITED v. CYPRUS

assessment.Existence of an interference: There was an interference with the applicants’ freedom of expression. The first applicant wrote the impugned newspaper column and the second applicant published it (see paragraph 6). Following civil defamation proceedings, the domestic courts found the article defamatory and ordered the applicants to pay EUR 12,000 in damages plus interest (see paragraphs 11 and 16). A civil judgment and damages award against a journalist and publisher for a press article plainly amount to an interference under Article 10.

assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference appears to have been prescribed by law. The domestic courts relied on the Cypriot law of defamation, and the available defences of truth and fair comment were expressly regulated by section 19 of the Civil Wrongs Law (Cap. 148) (see paragraph 18). The proceedings were conducted under that legal framework and the courts explained why, in their view, the applicants could not rely on those defences (see paragraphs 12-16). There is nothing in the facts suggesting that the interference lacked a sufficient basis in domestic law.

assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The interference pursued a legitimate aim, namely the protection of the reputation or rights of others. C.K. complained that the article damaged his personal and professional reputation and portrayed him as acting against the national interest and bargaining with thieves (see paragraph 9). The domestic courts likewise considered that the article attacked both his dignity and his professional standing as a lawyer (see paragraphs 12 and 16). This falls squarely within the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation or rights of others.

assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: The decisive issue is proportionality, and on the facts the interference was unlikely to be necessary in a democratic society. The article concerned a matter of obvious public interest: property in the occupied areas, the Cyprus problem, and the conduct of persons involved in litigation touching those issues (see paragraphs 6, 10 and 13). Under the Court’s case-law, expression on matters of public interest attracts a high level of protection, and the balancing exercise must consider contribution to a debate of general interest, the status of the person concerned, the form of the expression, and the severity of the sanction (see nos. 39954/08, 40660/08, 60641/08). Although the domestic courts treated C.K. as a private person (see paragraphs 14 and 16), he had himself entered the public arena by publishing in a prominent newspaper an article on the recovery of family paintings in the occupied territories and by acting as a lawyer in important property litigation (see paragraphs 5, 6 and 12). He therefore had to tolerate wider criticism than an ordinary private individual. Moreover, much of the impugned language was evaluative and polemical—such as references to dignity, ransom, or bargaining with thieves—used in a newspaper column engaging in public debate (see paragraph 6). Such value judgments need a sufficient factual basis, not proof of literal truth. Here, that basis existed in C.K.’s own published account that he had paid money to recover one painting and replaced another with a forgery (see paragraphs 5 and 10). The domestic courts focused narrowly on whether C.K. had literally “bought” the painting and faulted the journalist for not contacting him before commenting on an article already publicly authored by him (see paragraphs 12, 13 and 16). That approach gave insufficient weight to press freedom and to the accepted degree of exaggeration and provocation in public-interest commentary, especially where a lawyer’s conduct in a matter of public concern is criticised (see no. 29369/10). Even if the language was harsh, the reasons relied on domestically do not appear sufficiently relevant and sufficient to justify imposing civil liability on both applicants; the damages award was also capable of having a chilling effect on the press (see paragraph 11). Accordingly, the interference was not necessary in a democratic society.
